title: Token-Budget-Aware Chunker
summary: Build a text chunker that respects a token budget, adds configurable overlap, and never silently truncates mid-sentence.
requirements: Accept an array of words, a max-tokens-per-chunk budget, an overlap size, and a token estimator function.
Never drop a word, even one that alone exceeds the budget.
Apply overlap consistently at every chunk boundary except the last.
Return an array of chunks (each an array of words).
start: Start from Module 2's exercise function and add a real token estimator (characters/4, or a real tokenizer library if you want to go further) instead of the 1-token-per-word test mock.
acceptance: A generous budget produces one chunk containing everything.
A tight budget produces multiple chunks, each respecting the token limit.
An oversized single word still gets its own chunk, never dropped.
Overlap words appear at the end of one chunk AND the start of the next, consistently.
Every word from the input appears in at least one output chunk (full coverage, verified programmatically, not just visually).
tests: 20-word input, generous budget → 1 chunk, all 20 words.
20-word input, tight budget → multiple chunks, verify total unique words covered equals 20.
A single word with an estimated token count far exceeding the budget → its own chunk, not dropped.
Zero overlap → chunks partition cleanly with no repeated words.
Overlap=2 → verify the last 2 words of chunk N equal the first 2 words of chunk N+1.
mistakes: Enforcing the budget check even on an empty chunk, silently dropping an oversized word.
Off-by-one in the overlap math causing the last few words to be dropped on longer inputs.
Testing only with tiny inputs where an overlap bug wouldn't surface.
solution: Walk words with two pointers, building the current chunk until adding the next word would exceed budget (only enforced once the chunk is non-empty).
Start the next chunk at `max(current chunk start + 1, end - overlap)`.
Stop when a chunk reaches the end of the input.
Verify full coverage by collecting all words across all output chunks into a Python `set` and comparing its length against the input length.
